content: Paying blood donors can increase the likelihood of individuals from key populations, who may have limited access to other income sources, donating blood. However, this practice raises concerns about the potential for individuals with undiagnosed HIV infection to donate blood during the window period—the time shortly after infection when antibodies are not yet detectable. This could result in false-negative HIV test results, thereby posing a risk to blood recipients. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all blood donations undergo screening for HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and syphilis before being used for transfusions. National programs must ensure they have the capacity and resources to screen 100% of blood units used for transfusions, as this is the expected standard for a functional national blood supply system. HIV co-infection exacerbates the severity of infections caused by HBV and HCV. Without antiretroviral therapy (ART), co-infection increases the risk of death from liver-related conditions such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. It also reduces the effectiveness of hepatitis C treatment. The 2019 WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of routine HBV and HCV screening for people living with HIV to ensure proper management of co-infections. Since 2016, the Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) survey has included indicators for HBV and HCV screening among people living with HIV who are initiating ART. The widespread use of tenofovir-based ART regimens, which are effective against HBV, has reduced the necessity of HBV screening for initial clinical management. However, if ART regimens are changed, discontinuation of tenofovir should be avoided in individuals who are HBsAg-positive. Condom use during high-risk sexual activities is a critical indicator of protected versus unprotected sex. It reflects community norms, condom availability, and individual motivation to prevent HIV transmission. Surveys and health facility records are used to measure condom use among various populations, including the general population, sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and people who inject drugs. These data help monitor trends and inform HIV prevention strategies. The distribution of condoms is another important metric. National programs analyze the number of condoms distributed through different channels, such as the public sector, social marketing, and commercial sales, to optimize investments and ensure availability. Data on condom distribution are typically collected from program records and central warehouse stock reports. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) uptake is an essential measure of HIV prevention efforts. It reflects awareness and interest in reducing HIV risk through antiretroviral use. PrEP uptake is tracked by counting the number of eligible individuals who initiate PrEP during a reporting period. This includes first-time users and those who restart PrEP after discontinuation. Disaggregated data by age, gender, and population type help identify gaps and improve program targeting. Oral PrEP dosing strategies include daily use and event-driven dosing, the latter being recommended only for men who have sex with men. At the time of PrEP initiation, healthcare providers may inquire about the preferred dosing strategy to tailor interventions effectively.
